title: Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - Proper Redaction
subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: When fulfilling a public records request, an agency discovers that a vendor's proposal contains legitimate trade secrets, specifically a proprietary chemical formula. The agency must:
options: Deny the public records request in its entirety.
Release the document but request the citizen not to share the formula.
Redact only the specific formula from the document and release the remainder of the proposal.
Contact the vendor and allow them to sue the requester.
questions.explain: If a record contains both exempt and non-exempt material, the agency has a duty to redact (obscure) only the specific exempt information (the formula) and disclose the rest of the public record.

questions.q: In the digital age, which of the following represents an improper and legally risky method of redacting electronic PDF documents?
options: Using dedicated redaction software that permanently scrubs the underlying metadata.
Drawing a black box over the text using standard markup tools without flattening or removing the hidden text layer.
Printing the document, using a black marker, scanning it back to PDF, and destroying the original.
Replacing the text with an explicit label marking it '[REDACTED]'
questions.explain: Simply drawing a black shape over text in a standard PDF does not remove the underlying text layer. Requesters can easily copy and paste the hidden text, resulting in a data breach. Proper redaction requires permanently scrubbing the data.

questions.q: Many public solicitations explicitly require bidders to submit both a complete proposal and a separate 'Redacted Copy' for public release. If the vendor fails to submit the redacted copy, what is the usual legal consequence stated in the solicitation?
options: The agency will redact the document for them for a fee.
The vendor assumes all risk, and the agency may release the full, unredacted proposal in response to a public records request.
The proposal becomes voidable by the state attorney general.
The vendor's competitors can claim the proprietary data as their own.
questions.explain: Solicitations typically place the burden of claiming confidentiality on the vendor. If a vendor fails to supply a properly redacted copy as instructed, they waive their right to confidentiality, and the agency is legally authorized to release the full document.

questions.q: Before releasing a redacted procurement document to a competitor, the procurement officer notices that the vendor redacted their financial audited statements, which are protected under state law. The procurement officer should:
options: Proceed with releasing the redacted copy, as the financial data is legally exempt.
Unredact the financials to promote absolute transparency.
Send the document to the FBI for review.
Reject the vendor's bid for being too secretive.
questions.explain: Audited financial statements submitted to prove vendor capability are frequently shielded by state public records exemptions to protect private financial security. Retaining the vendor's redactions here is appropriate.

questions.q: A procurement office is releasing vendor employee resumes via a public records request. The resumes contain personal home addresses, personal cell phone numbers, and Social Security Numbers. This information is collectively known as:
options: Trade Secrets
Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (PCII)
Personally Identifiable Information (PII), which must be redacted to protect privacy.
Public Knowledge
questions.explain: PII (Personally Identifiable Information) includes SSNs, personal phone numbers, and home addresses. Most public records laws mandate the redaction of sensitive PII to protect individuals from identity theft and privacy invasions.

questions.q: After evaluating proposals, an agency issues a Notice of Intent to Award. A competitor requests the winning proposal. The winning vendor insists the entire proposal is confidential and threatens to sue the agency if anything is released. To legally navigate this, the agency should:
options: Submit to the vendor's threat and deny the public records request.
Inform the vendor of the impending release and provide a short window (e.g., 10 days) for the vendor to seek a protective order or injunction from a judge.
Arrest the vendor for interfering with public operations.
Cancel the entire procurement and start over.
questions.explain: When a vendor asserts aggressive confidentiality claims that conflict with public records laws, standard legal practice is to inform the vendor of the agency's intent to release the documents unless the vendor secures a court-issued protective order within a specified timeframe.
